text: A corpse lies in the Brahmin quarter of Durvasapura, and no one will touch it. Narayanappa ate meat, drank liquor and took a prostitute into his house, and Madhwa custom still requires that his rites be performed at once, by someone. Pattabhirama Reddy sets the film inside that stall: one agrahara, one body, one argument circling the same courtyard while the heat does its own work. The interest is not the dead man but the tone of voice his neighbours use when they quote scripture at each other. Orthodoxy here is procedure rather than belief, and the procedure has met a case it cannot file. A hundred and thirteen minutes in Kannada, 1969, and much of it is men waiting for another man to move first, an argument conducted largely through who declines to speak.

A bird catcher who cannot stand the sight of a cage is, as a livelihood, a contradiction. Lakhindar works the forests of Bengal, traps what he is paid to trap, and then opens his hands; the money that should follow the birds to market never reaches his door, and it is his wife who keeps the accounts of that decision. Buddhadeb Dasgupta gives the story eighty-two minutes, short enough that the poverty registers not as episodes but as weather — the same hut, the same empty pot, the same man home at dusk with nothing and a clear conscience. The middleman who carries the catch to town stays close by, and staying close by is his entire method. What the film weighs is not the tenderness but its price, and the price is charged to someone who never agreed to it.

Vishwam and Sita leave both families to marry, and the film starts where the romance would usually end: a rented room, a new town, the question of money not yet asked. Adoor Gopalakrishnan spends the next two hours watching that question arrive. Kerala, 1971, in Malayalam, and the couple's happiness is real for exactly as long as their small reserve lasts; the camera's attention goes to the arithmetic beneath it, the rent that falls due whether or not anyone has found work. Eloping takes an afternoon. What follows is a sequence of much smaller decisions, each made with less room than the one before, and Gopalakrishnan films them with the same evenness he gave the first — no scene arranged to tell the couple they were wrong.

Thirty thousand people answer an advertisement for a hundred jobs. Mrinal Sen builds the film out of that ratio and refuses to shrink it to one applicant's story: the crowd at the gate is the subject, and the camera keeps stepping aside to the photographer hunting a picture, the moneylender doing steady trade off the waiting, the police who cannot shape a line, the company posting vacancies while its own strike runs into a sixth month. India, 1973, in Bengali, and the register is not documentary — Sen allows himself fable, a scale and a tone that realism would not permit. The arithmetic holds it together. A hundred openings against thirty thousand pairs of hands means the outcome is settled before the gate opens, and everyone in the frame has already done the sum.

The adoptive parents are educated, patient and entirely reasonable, and that is the pressure. A well-off couple takes a sixteen-year-old out of a West Berlin orphanage in 1967 and sets about settling him into a household where every rule arrives as a suggestion and no refusal is allowed to mean anything. Johannes Schaaf runs it to eighty-six minutes, tight enough that the courtesies begin to repeat, and the repetition is the point. The boy comes with a history and no vocabulary for the one on offer; the adults have a therapeutic word for everything he does, which turns each of his acts into a symptom. Tätowierung went out as West Germany's international submission to the Academy Awards, a measure of how seriously a country can take a story about its own good manners.

Once a year Ghunuram takes leave from his job, has the stripes painted on and becomes a tiger for his village. The Tiger Dance works because everyone watching knows the man inside it; they are looking at a neighbour and an animal at the same time. Then a circus arrives with a leopard in a cage, newly caught and entirely real. Buddhadeb Dasgupta lets the two attractions stand side by side for a while without comment, which is the hardest thing he could do to his performer. Ninety-one minutes, a Bengali village in 1988, and beneath the rivalry sits an ordinary hope: Ghunuram means to marry the daughter of a fellow dancer, and her attention has begun to travel. A painted man against a caged animal is not a fair contest, and the village will settle it by looking.

The case turns on a receipt that was never written, and the man demanding it knows exactly that. A landlord asks Rakeshwar Bora to produce the paper proving his mortgage, and from that missing sheet an Assamese farmer's household comes apart in instalments — livestock sold to pay the men who move a file, a son sent into service in the house of the man taking the land. Jahnu Barua shot this in Assamese in 1986 and gave it two hours, roughly the pace of an agricultural year. He is careful never to let the landlord become a monster; the machinery does the work, and the machinery is lawful. The film follows what a man does when he is asked for something impossible that he is not permitted to refuse, and counts what he sells along the way.

He is thirteen when the state takes custody, and from then on the file moves faster than the boy. Martin steals and likes stealing, and he admires an older brother who is not around to complicate the admiration; the homes he passes through read each refusal as evidence and write incorrigible where a reason should be. Norbert Kückelmann made this in West Germany in 1979, a hundred and five minutes at the temperature of a case report, and its curiosity is administrative rather than sentimental — how a system built to rescue a child comes to require that the child perform being rescued. The adults are not villains. They have forms, caseloads, waiting lists and a vocabulary in which a runaway is a category. One psychologist tries something else, which the institution can permit but not repeat.

Germany, 1953, and the man at the centre is an officer of the Russian army. Victor Vicas builds ninety-five minutes on one unfinished thing: a girl the officer met during the war and has not managed to put down. The war itself is present as memory rather than spectacle, which is what the word haunted commits a film to. Eight years after the fighting, in a country living next door to its own recent history, the choice of protagonist carries weight before a scene has played — sympathy pointed across a line that was hardening while the picture was being made. The premise is bare and stays bare, which puts the load on interior work: how much of a life arranged around orders a memory can occupy, and what a soldier does with an attachment nobody has authorised him to keep.

Tabara Shetty gives his working life to the government, and the trouble begins on the day it no longer needs him. Girish Kasaravalli takes that hinge — a career ends, and the ordinary supports under a household turn out to have been provisional — and gives it a hundred and ten minutes in Kannada. The man knows how the offices work; he spent decades inside them. Knowing does not help. Then his wife, who is his only company, falls sick, and the difficulty stops being an inconvenience and becomes a schedule. Kasaravalli films clerks and corridors with the patience other directors reserve for weather, and the effect accumulates rather than climaxes: dignity is not taken from Tabara Shetty in a single scene, it is spent.

The kingdom of Yue loses its war and answers with a gift: a woman sent to the victor's court, beautiful and briefed. That is the machine Li Han-Hsiang set running after leaving Shaw Brothers in Hong Kong for Taiwan, where he mounted a production larger than the industry there was accustomed to attempting — 154 minutes, the Warring States, a defeated king rebuilding at home while his conqueror is kept comfortably occupied. Xishi's work at the court of Wu is domestic and unending: audiences, favours, entertainments, the steady subtraction of a ruler's attention from his own governance. The film is far more interested in that daily labour than in troop movements, and it lets a palace be a workplace with shifts and duties. It took the Golden Horse for best feature.

The dialogue is in Sanskrit, and the film asks its audience to sit inside a language most of them will hear rather than follow. G. V. Iyer set that condition in 1991 and then had to sustain a hundred and forty minutes inside it, adapting the Bhagavad Gita — an epic of two families and a throne only one of them can hold. Every part of the choice is hard. Performers must carry meaning in sound before sense, and the drama has to hold through a sacred text without being converted into ordinary movie speech. Iyer treats the language as the performance rather than an obstacle to it, letting recitation set the rhythm that music would set elsewhere. India's National Film Award for best feature went to it, which says the wager was at least legible at the time.

A pair of bullocks, found straying in the forest and kept, is the nearest thing Choma has to a future. He is not permitted to put them to his own field: bonded to a landlord, born into a caste that may work land but not hold it, he does the arithmetic anyway, and the animals stand in the yard as a plan with no legal route out of it. Missionaries arrive with an offer that includes land and requires a conversion, and his refusal is the costliest thing in the film. B.V. Karanth shot it in Kannada in 1974 and let it run past two hours, unhurried in the way that lets an impossibility settle rather than announce itself. Choma has a drum. It is the one place his anger is permitted to go, and Karanth keeps coming back to the sound of it.

In a district town small enough to hold exactly two powers, one of them is a doctor. Dr. Mukherjee runs the civil surgery, treats the poor of a tribal district and is trusted by them well past the point of medicine; the other power is Laxman Lal, an aristocrat's son who has never been told no. Tapan Sinha keeps the collision domestic rather than heroic. A widow who wants Laxman Lal to leave her alone takes shelter in the doctor's house, and the tension comes from the plain fact that a house is not a fortress and a reputation is not armour. Bengali, 1966, a hundred and thirty-three minutes, much of it spent on rounds — small ailments, small debts, small negotiations — because that is where Sinha locates the doctor's standing and the exact thing that makes it fragile.
